results.conclusion: A Kestrel statement dated 2 September 2026 says Phase 2 reached its rated capacity on 28 August 2026. The statement gives no unit figures. A second statement dated 20 September 2026 says the plant operated at 92 per cent of rated capacity in the week ending 18 September 2026. The record states no customer lead times. On May 15, 2026, the regional transmission organization covering the eastern interconnection published its daily demand forecast. The forecast projected a peak load of 118,400 megawatts for the operating day ending May 16, 2026. The same notice reported a preliminary peak of 116,900 megawatts for May 14, 2026. A separate filing from the western balancing authority stated that its operating reserve margin stood at 14.2 percent as of 06:00 local time on May 15, 2026. The filing cited a total available capacity of 82,300 megawatts against a forecast peak of 72,100 megawatts. No emergency declarations were issued by either organization for the period covered. Combined reported capacity for the four operators is 38,100 units a month at the end of Q3 2026, against 33,100 units a month at the end of Q2 2026. Combined reported Q3 2026 output is 104,700 units. The record states no customer lead times. Combined reported capacity for the two operators is 7,400 units a month at the end of Q3 2026, unchanged from the end of Q2 2026. Combined reported Q3 2026 output is 22,200 units. The record states no customer lead times. The Malaysia Semiconductor Industry Association released its Q3 2026 packaging summary on 25 September 2026. The summary lists six reporting members and gives a combined capacity of 45,500 units a month at the end of Q3 2026. It gives a combined output of 126,900 units for the quarter. The association notes that two members did not file Q3 2026 figures. The Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry published an update on 18 September 2026 covering approved advanced-packaging projects. The update lists four approved projects with a combined planned capacity of 21,000 units a month. It gives no commissioning dates. At the end of Q2 2026, reported capacity for the six operators covered by the association summary was 40,500 units a month. At the end of Q3 2026 it was 45,500 units a month. The change is 5,000 units a month. Kestrel's Phase 2 plant accounts for the whole of the change. The independent system operator for the central region published its day-ahead market results for May 15, 2026. The average locational marginal price for the on-peak period was 34.12 dollars per megawatt-hour. The off-peak average was 26.78 dollars per megawatt-hour. The maximum hourly price was 61.50 dollars per megawatt-hour, recorded at hour ending 17:00. The minimum was 18.90 dollars per megawatt-hour at hour ending 04:00. Scheduled interchange with neighboring balancing authorities totaled 3,450 megawatts for the peak hour. A separate report from the southwest power pool indicated that its market clearing price for the same day averaged 29.45 dollars per megawatt-hour.

results.question: Which EscrowCreate field lets the sender recover locked funds if the escrow is never finished?
results.conclusion: XRPL escrow locks funds until its time or cryptographic conditions permit release; it does not judge whether purchased prose is useful or true. EscrowCreate establishes the obligation, EscrowFinish releases it when requirements are satisfied, and EscrowCancel returns an expired escrow's funds when cancellation succeeds. Expiration alone does not submit that cancellation transaction. [1] Time-based, conditional and combined escrows express different release constraints. A condition can bind release to a cryptographic fulfillment, while FinishAfter and CancelAfter control time windows. The documentation describes ledger objects that persist until completion or cancellation. A browser countdown is consequently an estimate of eligibility, not proof that the object was removed or the sender recovered funds. [1] For encrypted information sales, my recommendation is to bind the agreed ciphertext, condition and delivered passage commitments before paying. A revealed key may satisfy a cryptographic condition without establishing factual accuracy. Preserve that distinction in dispute handling. A refund after completed release requires a separate mechanism; do not assume cancellation can undo an already finished escrow. [1] Test a valid fulfillment, an incorrect fulfillment, a seller that never finishes and a validated cancellation after expiry. Reconcile the exact escrow owner and sequence before retrying. Preserve transaction references rather than treating a network timeout as failure. These recommendations follow the lifecycle described in the source; they make no claim that a particular application has implemented semantic arbitration or unilateral refunds. [1]

results.question: What must a holder submit before an account can receive an issued token such as a stablecoin on XRPL?
results.conclusion: XRPL issuers can claw back eligible issued tokens when the required controls are enabled, but native XRP cannot be clawed back. The documentation distinguishes trust-line token controls from MPT issuance flags. Clawback is an issuer capability, not a general right for any dissatisfied buyer to reverse a payment. [1] For trust-line tokens, Allow Clawback must be configured under the documented account restrictions before issuance. The documentation also describes incompatibility with the No Freeze setting. MPTs use an issuance-level capability. These different control surfaces are a reason to inspect the actual asset and issuer rather than treating all fungible tokens as interchangeable. [1] For an agent wallet, I recommend surfacing issuer control risk when selecting a payment asset. Separate a seller refund from an issuer clawback and from expiration-based escrow cancellation. A service should not promise automatic recovery merely because the token standard includes a clawback feature. Whether an issuer can or will act in a particular dispute needs separate legal and operational evidence. [1] Exercise the configured capability on a testing token, a token without it and a native XRP transaction. Record the issuer and issuance configuration used. Do not generalize from those tests to a named stablecoin without examining its real settings. These recommendations derive from the documented controls and intentionally avoid asserting that any issuer has a universal legal entitlement to recover funds in every jurisdiction. [1] A dedicated issuer creates TEST-SGD tokens on Testnet for experiments; these tokens carry no economic value and substitute for RLUSD only in mechanism tests. S$ prices map 1:1 to TEST-SGD; this is neither a peg nor a backing claim. Recovery is part of that liquidity story. CancelAfter permits cancellation after the validated ledger deadline; it does not automatically return funds. Policy must submit EscrowCancel and confirm successful validation before describing principal as returned. Fees remain spent. A refund after completed key publication is a different writer-signed Payment and requires writer cooperation. Throughout provisioning, purchase and recovery, the budget remains the spending authority and durable intent identity prevents duplicate principal purchases. These observations support bounded mechanism claims only. make testnet ARGS=--iou provisions a dedicated issuer with AccountSet flag 17, buyer/writer trust lines and a buyer issuance using only public-faucet-funded Testnet accounts. Seeds remain in the 0600 scratch wallet store. ESCROW_ASSET=test-iou is the equivalent environment switch (the launcher supplies TESTNET_IOU_ISSUER). XRP remains the default; MCP supports the opt-in --testnet --iou mode using TEST-SGD. See XLS-85 and xrpl.js flag 17. No mainnet support is claimed. - The writer receives the principal only by publishing K through a successful finish. A relay can submit the same fulfillment; funds still go to the original destination. Buyer cancellation is policy-only and cannot win before expiry. - K becomes public. This is acceptable because each ciphertext is encrypted for one buyer and intent with a fresh key; it does not unlock other buyers' copies. It is not DRM: anyone with that ciphertext and public K can read that copy. - A writer can commit to nonsense or an undecryptable envelope and collect. The cryptographic proof establishes responsibility, not truth or automatic damages. Existing challenges/reputation handle broken promises; this is not a truth oracle. - K may appear in an unvalidated submitted finish. The buyer still waits for validation. Ledger outages/history gaps retain reservations pending reconciliation. - A dishonest buyer can create extra escrow objects outside policy. This product guarantees one charge per policy intent, not control of arbitrary wallet activity. - Conditional finish costs more than a Payment. The XRPL fee formula scales as base_fee × (33 + fulfillment_bytes / 16) before multisign/load effects. Here K is 32 bytes and its encoded fulfillment is 36 bytes. At the observed 12-drop signing base, ceil(12 × (33 + 36/16)) = 423 drops. A 2,000-drop cap rejects excessive fees. Live create/cancel each cost 12 drops. A cancelled 60,000-drop principal is fully returned; its buyer still pays 24 drops in fees. - Synthetic corpus and extractive fixture answers in the proof are labelled; Testnet value transfer is real Testnet execution, with no real value.

results.question: Why does every trust line make a wallet need more XRP than just the transaction fee?
results.conclusion: An XRPL wallet needs a base reserve plus applicable owner reserves, separately from the money it intends to send. The reserve documentation lists Mainnet settings of 1 XRP per account and 0.2 XRP per owned item at access time, and warns that other networks can differ. Validators can change requirements through fee voting; these figures are a dated reference, not a permanent application constant. [1] Base reserve supports the account's existence; owner reserve constrains ledger objects. Escrows, offers and signer lists can affect the latter. Removing an object can release its reserve requirement. Reserves are not payments to validators, and the documentation permits reserved XRP to pay transaction costs. Treating every XRP in a balance as transferable would therefore confuse several distinct accounting concepts. [1] For an agent builder, my recommendation is to estimate spendable XRP from validated account state and the network's reserve settings before authorizing a payment. Include pending object creation in that estimate. A wallet with enough principal for a purchase may still lack room for the escrow object or transaction fee. Report the failed prerequisite precisely rather than silently switching assets or increasing funding authority. [1] Test provisioning with an account near its required reserve, an additional owned object, and removal of that object. Keep the funding source and network in the experiment record. The documentation's special treatment of initial trust lines is another reason to query actual state rather than assume that every account has the same object cost. This is an integration recommendation derived from reserve mechanics, not evidence that a particular deployed wallet passed those cases. [1]

results.question: Which XRPL transaction publishes or updates a decentralized identifier for an account?
results.conclusion: An XLS-40 decentralized identifier identifies a controller and supports verifiable associations, but does not by itself prove a person's legal identity. XRPL's DID documentation explicitly distinguishes a self-created identifier from assertions validated by a trusted credential issuer. An identifier's existence and the truth of claims about its owner require separate evidence. [1] [2] XLS-40 specifies the XRPL DID method and operations for managing DID data. A DID document can supply verification information or refer to externally stored material. The documentation describes resolving a document and checking a credential as distinct steps. A working URI proves neither that an issuer is trustworthy nor that every assertion in the referenced document is current. [1] [2] For an agent marketplace, I recommend keeping controller authentication separate from identity verification and reputation. Verify signatures for the operation being requested, then evaluate issuer policy and credential validity for any identity claim. A seller should not gain a credibility boost merely by creating a DID. Handle broken external references as unavailable evidence rather than automatically substituting a self-description. [1] [2] Test document updates, deleted references and a credential from an issuer the verifier does not trust. Record which public keys and document version were used for verification. Avoid putting sensitive identity evidence in a public ledger simply to make a demonstration easier. These are implementation recommendations grounded in the DID model, not a declaration that a DID constitutes KYC approval or that an identifier owner holds any particular licence. [1] [2]

results.question: What is the maximum trading fee an XRPL AMM pool can set?
results.conclusion: The XLS-30 AMM adds liquidity pools to the XRPL DEX alongside order books, and routing can consider both sources of liquidity. Liquidity providers receive pool interests represented by LP tokens. Providing liquidity is an economic position with risks, not an assurance that every future exchange will have a favorable price. [1] [2] The specification describes a geometric-mean market maker, trading fees, LP governance and an auction mechanism for trading advantages. Payment and order operations can combine pool and order-book liquidity. These mechanisms describe how exchange opportunities are formed; they do not make a price quote timeless or remove the importance of token issuer identity. [1] [2] For an agent buyer, I recommend separating buying research from supplying liquidity. If conversion is needed, bound source spending and required destination delivery explicitly. Examine trading costs and available liquidity before authorizing a route. Do not infer that an application's stablecoin can be redeemed at par merely because an AMM offers a trading pair for it. [1] [2] An integration experiment should compare a bounded trade with its actual validated balance changes and identify the pool and assets involved. Include insufficient liquidity and an adverse price change. LP testing should separately examine deposit and withdrawal behavior rather than reuse a trader's success criterion. These are suggested engineering checks derived from the AMM design, not investment advice, a return forecast or proof that a named production pool has been audited. [1] [2]

results.question: Which Payment field lets an agent pay in one currency while the recipient receives another through the DEX or AMMs?
results.conclusion: Recovery is part of that liquidity story. CancelAfter permits cancellation after the validated ledger deadline; it does not automatically return funds. Policy must submit EscrowCancel and confirm successful validation before describing principal as returned. Fees remain spent. A refund after completed key publication is a different writer-signed Payment and requires writer cooperation. Throughout provisioning, purchase and recovery, the budget remains the spending authority and durable intent identity prevents duplicate principal purchases. These observations support bounded mechanism claims only. Asset provisioning and buying research are separate operations. The builder feedback records dated Testnet observations rather than a current mainnet survey. That distinction is essential for stablecoins: a successful direct token payment does not prove that the same issuer permits token escrow. A wallet balance does not establish that an agent may spend it, and a price displayed in SGD is not an independently measured foreign exchange rate. The basic purchase contract requires an expected network, asset and issuer before policy signs. XRP uses integer drops, with one million drops per XRP. An issued asset also needs the currency and issuer identity; the currency name alone is insufficient. The buyer checks destination, exact amount, invoice binding, expiry and policy limits. Validated settlement must show successful delivery. The requested Amount alone does not prove what arrived, particularly for partial payments. These are payment validation requirements, not decisions delegated to the language model. Token escrow adds issuer requirements beyond holding an issued balance. The builder feedback's 7 November entry B26 records an earlier validated observation: TokenEscrow was enabled, but the official RLUSD Testnet issuer flags lacked AllowTrustLineLocking. The documented implication was that official RLUSD escrow was blocked by issuer permission. The record distinguishes that code-derived blocker from an actually submitted rejection transaction. A trust line does not supply missing issuer consent. Recheck the issuer and network before claiming present support; this article itself performs no fresh ledger query. The available workaround is explicit about substitution. XRP remains the default key-reveal asset, while TEST-SGD is a labelled issued-token stand-in for experiments. TEST-SGD is not official RLUSD and does not demonstrate RLUSD issuer cooperation. Direct RLUSD Testnet payments and conditional token escrow are separate evidence classes. A report should identify which it tested, with the exact transaction hash and issuer, rather than describing every successful token transaction as proof of the same settlement mode. Nothing here is redeemable money or a production stablecoin guarantee. Funding observations also need labels. The 3 November builder feedback records public RLUSD faucet authentication friction and historical bounded native Testnet DEX provisioning. In those samples, acquisition cost about 25.1 Testnet XRP for two RLUSD. That arbitrary test exchange rate is not economic evidence. The workaround used an exact self-payment, a bounded SendMax and a fee cap, checked validated delivered_amount, and kept provisioning separate from product purchases. It does not establish an automatic exchange strategy for the research agent or an available mainnet funding route. A DEX provisioning observation likewise does not establish AMM behavior. The cited repository evidence concerns acquiring a test balance, not measuring pool pricing, liquidity provision or agent routing through an AMM. No AMM performance result is claimed here. When evaluating agent payments, ask which asset was already provisioned, which exact asset policy authorized, and whether conversion happened outside the purchase loop. Do not infer a pool mechanism from an exchange label. This boundary prevents a setup workaround from becoming an unsupported product capability claim. Fees and reserves constrain even faucet-funded micropayments. Builder feedback B19 records 12-drop create and cancel fees and a 423-drop conditional finish using xrpl.js 4.7.0. Its observed OwnerCount changed from zero to one and back to zero with a 0.2 XRP increment. These are dated measurements, not universal fee quotes. A wallet needs terminal transaction fee headroom and object reserve liquidity as well as purchase principal. The number of concurrent escrow objects can therefore constrain capacity independently of article prices or burned network fees.

results.question: Which Singapore statute governs digital payment token services that an XRPL payments product could fall under?
results.conclusion: Singapore payment-service obligations depend on the service and applicable legal scope, not on whether an agent or XRPL submits the transaction. MAS describes the Payment Services Act as regulating payment-service providers and payment systems. A token's foreign regulatory status does not establish a Singapore application's permission to provide a regulated service. [1] [2] [3] MAS's September 2026 stablecoin announcement describes consultation on legislative amendments, including the framework for qualifying MAS-regulated stablecoins. It covers Singapore-issued single-currency stablecoins pegged to SGD or a G10 currency and discusses proposals concerning foreign issuance. A consultation proposal should not be reported as a licence already granted to a particular issuer. [1] [2] [3] For a builder, my recommendation is to map the actual activities: custody, exchange, transfer, issuance and who serves which customers. Associate each activity with the responsible entity and applicable legal review. Do not label a stablecoin MAS-regulated solely because it tracks USD, runs on XRPL or has supervision elsewhere. Keep product claims bounded by dated official evidence. [1] [2] [3] Before deployment, prepare a service-flow description that identifies asset control and customer relationships. Check current legislation, MAS guidance and the relevant entity's permissions against that flow. These are compliance-scoping recommendations rather than a legal conclusion about this project. The article does not identify an approved bank partner, promise a regulatory exemption or claim that a successful testing transaction demonstrates production authorization. [1] [2] [3]
